title: Housing Navigator
subtitle: Renting, tenant rights, and avoiding housing scams.
landingBody: Learn all about housing in California.

sections.title: Welcome
sections.body:
Renting or buying in California comes with challenges. Rules, paperwork, and costs can feel unfamiliar, especially if you are new to the US.

Continue reading to learn about rental requirements, other ways to qualify, trusted housing resources, tenant rights, and how to avoid housing scams.

If at any time you feel lost, ask the AI at the bottom of the screen. It can explain the current section in simpler words or answer a question about your situation.

sections.title: Understand rental requirements
sections.intro: Most landlords ask for the same basic items when you apply to rent. Gathering them ahead of time makes applying faster and less stressful. Here is what each one usually means.

topics.heading: Rental application
topics.paragraph: This is the form the landlord or property manager uses to collect your information. It usually asks for your full name, current and past addresses, phone number, email, employment details, income, and the names of everyone who will live in the unit. Some forms are on paper and some are online. Fill it out carefully and use the same name that appears on your ID. Keep a copy or screenshot of what you submit so you remember what you shared.

topics.heading: Photo ID
topics.paragraph: Landlords need a government issued photo ID to confirm who you are. A passport, US driver license, state ID, or another official photo ID is usually accepted. Bring the original to show in person, and ask before you send copies online. Only share ID images through a trusted application portal or directly with the property office, not through random text or social media messages.

topics.heading: Proof of income
topics.paragraph: This shows you can pay the rent each month. Common proof includes recent pay stubs, an offer letter with your salary, bank statements, tax forms, or a letter from your employer. Many landlords look for monthly income of about two to three times the rent, but policies vary. If you are paid in cash, self employed, or new to a job, ask what documents they will accept. Print or save clear copies so you can upload or hand them in quickly.

topics.heading: References
topics.paragraph: References are people the landlord can contact to learn whether you are reliable. Past landlords are the most useful. If you have never rented in the US, you can often use an employer, teacher, case worker, or community organization contact instead. Ask permission first, then give their full name, relationship to you, phone number, and email. Tell your references that a landlord may call so they are ready to answer.

topics.heading: Credit and background checks
topics.paragraph: A credit check looks at how you have handled bills and loans in the US. A background check may look for eviction or criminal records. Newcomers often have little or no US credit history, which is common and not the same as bad credit. Ask the landlord what they check and what they do if someone has no US credit file. You usually authorize these checks on the application. In California, application screening fees are limited by law, and you can ask for a copy of any consumer report used to deny your application.

topics.heading: Application fee
topics.paragraph: This is a fee some landlords charge to cover screening costs such as credit or background checks. In California, the amount is capped and should only cover actual out of pocket screening costs. Ask whether the fee is required, how much it is, and whether it is refundable before you pay. Pay through the official office or portal, get a receipt, and never wire money or use gift cards to someone claiming to be a landlord.

sections.title: Learn alternative ways to qualify
sections.intro: Many newcomers do not have a US credit history yet. That does not always mean you cannot rent. Landlords sometimes accept other ways to show you are reliable. Ask what they allow, and consider these common options.

topics.heading: Co-signer or guarantor
topics.paragraph: A co-signer is someone with stronger credit or income who agrees to pay the rent if you cannot. This is often a relative, friend, or sponsor who lives in the US. The landlord will usually ask that person to fill out an application and pass a credit check too. Only ask someone you trust, and make sure they understand they are legally responsible if rent is unpaid.

topics.heading: Larger security deposit
topics.paragraph: Some landlords will accept a higher deposit when your credit history is short or missing. This is meant to lower their risk. California limits how much deposit a landlord can charge, so ask what is allowed for that unit. Get any deposit amount in writing, and keep proof of what you paid.

topics.heading: Proof of income or savings
topics.paragraph: Even without credit history, strong bank statements, pay stubs, or proof of savings can help. Some landlords want to see several months of income or enough money in the bank to cover rent for a set period. Bring clear, recent documents. If income comes from more than one source, include all of it and label what each document shows.

topics.heading: Employer or offer letter
topics.paragraph: A letter from your employer can confirm your job, start date, and pay. If you have a new job offer, the offer letter may work while you wait for your first pay stubs. Ask your employer or HR for a signed letter on company letterhead. Include a contact name and phone number the landlord can call to verify.

topics.heading: Newcomer and housing programs
topics.paragraph: Some nonprofits, resettlement agencies, and local housing programs help immigrants find rentals or connect with landlords who work with newcomers. These programs may offer application help, references, rental assistance, or lists of friendly properties. Ask at a library, community center, or immigrant services office near you about housing help in your language.

sections.title: Access housing resources
sections.intro: You do not have to figure out housing alone. Libraries, nonprofit counselors, and government sites can help you find rentals, learn the rules, and get local support. Here are a few trustworthy websites to start with.

topics.heading: HUD (US Department of Housing and Urban Development)
topics.paragraph: HUD is the main federal housing agency. Its website explains rental help, fair housing rules, and how to find approved housing counselors near you. Use it when you want official US government information.

topics.heading: HUD Find a Housing Counselor
topics.paragraph: This HUD tool helps you find a HUD approved housing counselor. Counselors can explain applications, budgets, and rental options. Many offer help by phone or in person, and some speak more than one language.

topics.heading: California Courts Self-Help Housing
topics.paragraph: This is the official California courts self help site for housing. It covers eviction, deposits, repairs, and other tenant issues in plain language. It is a good place to learn what the court process looks like if you have a housing problem.

topics.heading: California Landlord-Tenant Guide
topics.paragraph: The California Department of Consumer Affairs publishes a free landlord tenant guide. It explains deposits, rent increases, repairs, and notices. Read it when you want a clear overview of common rental rules in California.

topics.heading: California Housing and Community Development
topics.paragraph: California HCD shares state housing programs and consumer resources. Check this site for statewide housing information and links to help finding affordable options.

211 connects you to local health and human services, including housing and rental assistance in many areas. You can search online or dial 211 to ask about help near you in your language when it is available.

sections.title: Understand tenant rights
sections.intro: Tenants in California have important rights. Rules can vary by city, so always check local laws too. Here are the basics, explained one topic at a time.

topics.heading: Security deposits
topics.paragraph: A security deposit is money you pay up front that the landlord holds while you rent. It can cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear. California limits how much a landlord can charge. When you move out, the landlord must return what is left and give an itemized list of any deductions within the time the law requires. Take dated photos when you move in and when you leave so you have proof of the unit condition.

topics.heading: Repairs and livable housing
topics.paragraph: Your rental must be safe and livable. That usually includes working heat, plumbing, electricity, locks, and freedom from serious hazards like major leaks or pest infestations. Tell the landlord in writing when something needs repair, keep a copy, and give a reasonable time to fix it. If the problem is serious and ignored, look up your local options or talk to a housing counselor or legal aid group before you withhold rent or move out.

topics.heading: Privacy
topics.paragraph: You have a right to privacy in your home. In most cases a landlord must give advance notice before entering, except in emergencies. Ask what notice your lease and local law require. You can refuse entry that does not follow the rules. Keep a written record if a landlord enters without proper notice.

topics.heading: Eviction notices
topics.paragraph: A landlord generally cannot lock you out or shut off utilities to force you to leave. Eviction usually starts with a written notice and, if needed, a court case. Read any notice carefully, note the deadlines, and get help quickly from legal aid or a self help court site. Do not ignore court papers. Showing up and responding on time protects your rights.

topics.heading: Protection from discrimination
topics.paragraph: Federal and California fair housing laws ban discrimination based on things like race, national origin, religion, sex, disability, familial status, and other protected categories under state law. A landlord generally cannot refuse to rent, set different terms, or harass you for those reasons. If you think you were treated unfairly, you can contact HUD fair housing, California Civil Rights enforcement, or a local fair housing nonprofit for help.

sections.title: Avoid housing scams
sections.intro: Housing scams try to rush you into sending money or personal information before you can check that a rental is real. Here are common tricks, how they usually work, and how to spot them.

topics.heading: Wire money and gift card payments
topics.paragraph: A scammer may claim to be out of town and ask you to wire money, send a money order, use Zelle, crypto, or buy gift cards to hold the unit. Once the money is sent, it is often gone. Real landlords almost never ask for gift cards or urgent wires before a signed lease. Pay only through a known office or trusted portal, and get a written receipt.

topics.heading: Pay before you tour
topics.paragraph: Some scams demand a deposit, application fee, or first month rent before you have seen the place or met anyone from the property. They may say many people want it and you must pay today. A real rental process usually lets you view the unit first. If someone blocks a tour and still wants money, treat that as a warning.

topics.heading: Rentals you cannot visit
topics.paragraph: Scammers often post nice photos of a home they do not control. They may say the keys are with a relative, the unit is being remodeled, or you can only see it after you pay. You arrive later and find it was never for rent, or someone else already lives there. Insist on seeing the exact unit in person, or on a live video walkthrough with a verified agent, before sending money.

topics.heading: Fake listings and fake landlords
topics.paragraph: Stolen photos, copied ads, and fake landlord names appear on social media and listing sites. Prices that look far below the neighborhood average are a common lure. Check that the person can prove they own or manage the property. Look up the management company, visit the leasing office, and compare the listing to other ads for the same address. If details do not match, walk away.

topics.heading: Phishing for documents and identity
topics.paragraph: Scammers may send a link and ask for your passport, Social Security number, bank login, or ID photos through email, text, or chat. They can use that information to steal your identity or money. Only share sensitive documents through a landlord or portal you have verified. Never click unexpected links, and never send full ID packets to strangers who contacted you first.
